title: Sudanese Army Drones Kill Over 300 in Kordofan and Abyei as South Sudan Lodges a Formal Protest, Britain Sends Fighters to Saudi Arabia, and Japan Puts a 1,000km Missile on Yonaguni
subhead: A three-day wave of Sudanese army drone strikes has killed more than 300 people, including 153 in the disputed Abyei market, pushing Khartoum and Juba into open confrontation. Britain is now flying defensive combat air patrols over Saudi cities, and Japan has deployed its first long-range land-to-ship missile to the island 110km from Taiwan.

sections.heading: Sudan's Drone War Crosses Into Abyei
sections.body:
Sudanese army drone strikes over the weekend and Monday killed more than 300 people across West Kordofan and the disputed Abyei region, according to reporting by BBC Verify and DW. In Abyei, a drone hit the Amiet Market west of the town at around midday on Monday; the region's caretaker information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor, told Reuters and the AP that the toll had risen from 73 to at least 153 by Tuesday. BBC Verify reviewed satellite imagery showing extensive burnt buildings in the market's north-east corner.

A separate strike hit a truck carrying roughly 200 mourners near Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, plus a funeral tent, killing about 145 people, according to the Sudan War Observatory; a third strike hit a market in Al-Mujlad the same evening. Sudan's army has not denied the Abyei strike — a military source told the BBC it targeted what it described as an RSF fuel supply site — but says it does not attack civilians.

The diplomatic fallout is the more significant part. Abyei is jointly administered by Sudan and South Sudan and sits on oil wealth left unsettled since Juba's 2011 independence, with the UN UNISFA mission in place for 15 years. South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador and demanded Khartoum stop actions endangering civilians; officials in Abyei and Juba dispute Khartoum's claim that the RSF operates from the territory. Both capitals now claim ownership of the same ground.
sections.whyItMatters: The war has jumped from an internal army-RSF fight into a Sudan-South Sudan flashpoint over an oil-bearing territory, with UN peacekeepers unable to prevent drone strikes. A border war there would compound the world's largest displacement crisis and put the region's oil infrastructure at risk.

sections.heading: Britain Flies Its Fighters Over Saudi Cities
sections.body:
Britain will run defensive counter-air missions over Saudi Arabia using RAF Typhoon fighters, Downing Street and the Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday, following a Saudi request after renewed Houthi attacks. Per the Guardian, the Typhoons are to be based in Qatar; a UK government statement confirmed an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity, alongside existing air-defence equipment and personnel. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the aircraft would operate defensively: 'These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.'

The trigger was a Houthi barrage the group claimed on Monday against the Aramco site at Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and the airports of Riyadh and Abha. Kpler counted at least 18 vessel attacks in the Gulf in a two-week period, and LSEG analysts noted that Iran has extended attacks as far south as the Gulf of Oman, hitting loadings and the ship-to-ship transfers that have kept Middle East volumes moving.

This is London joining the shooting war's defensive side, not the offensive one — a distinction it is emphasising because a Typhoon shootdown of a Houthi drone over Riyadh is now plausible.
sections.whyItMatters: A European air force is now committed to defending the world's largest oil exporter's cities and infrastructure. That raises the cost of Houthi escalation, but also the chance of a British casualty or engagement that pulls London deeper in.

sections.heading: Iran Hardens: No Talks, and a Third Tanker on a Mine
sections.body:
Iran's position hardened on two fronts on Tuesday. President Masoud Pezeshkian told Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, in Tehran that there would be no talks with Washington until Iranian demands are met, according to Nournews via the Straits Times. Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, while confirming indirect channels through Pakistan and Qatar remain open. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to US media, called a peace deal 'extremely difficult' and said economic pressure continues until Iran stops targeting commercial shipping, Al Jazeera reported.

The IRGC navy said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude caught fire after hitting a mine south of Hormuz — the third vessel to burn after striking mines in the waterway. In the energy market, Brent rose 0.78% to $109.64 a barrel on Wednesday after settling at $108.79 on Tuesday, having touched a five-month high of $111.99, Reuters reported via CNBC. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the gradual closure of all border crossings with Iran starting Wednesday with al-Sheib in Maysan, according to 964media — Baghdad putting distance between itself and Tehran.
sections.whyItMatters: Diplomacy is stalled on Iran's terms, shipping losses are accumulating, and oil is holding near $110. Iraq closing its Iranian border signals that even Tehran's neighbours are now hedging against it.

sections.heading: Keen Sword 27: A 1,000km Missile 110km From Taiwan
sections.body:
Japan and the United States began Keen Sword 27 on Monday, one of their largest joint exercises, with about 45,000 Japanese troops and 12,000 US personnel, running through next Thursday. Seven additional Indo-Pacific and European nations participate in parts of it, five for the first time: France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, the Japanese Joint Staff Office said, per the Taipei Times.

The deployment details matter more than the numbers. The Japan Self-Defence Force introduced its first Type-25 land-to-ship missile to Yonaguni — Japan's westernmost island, 110km east of Taiwan — with a range of roughly 1,000km. The US Navy-Marine Corps Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System are also on Yonaguni for the first time, with HIMARS on nearby Ishigaki. Japan's defence minister, Wellington Koo in Taipei, praised the inclusion of a Taiwan contingency scenario; Japan's joint staff chief, General Hiroaki Uchikura, denied the drills target any specific country.

The same day, Taiwan's defence ministry reported 29 PLA aircraft around the island in 24 hours, 23 of which crossed the median line into northern, central, south-western and eastern airspace, plus 6 navy vessels and 9 official ships.
sections.whyItMatters: Anti-ship missiles able to reach the Chinese mainland are now physically based on the island closest to Taiwan, with European navies participating for the first time. That is a real change in the pre-positioned force posture, not a symbolic exercise.

sections.heading: Witkoff to Moscow as Washington Squeezes Kyiv
sections.body:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff travels to Russia on Wednesday to meet Vladimir Putin, after what a US official called 'constructive' talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo that also involved the Norwegian and Finnish leaders and European and NATO representatives. The official told Reuters the talks covered security guarantees, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security order, and that participants made 'meaningful progress' toward a coordinated approach to Russia. Trump, speaking to reporters, said simply: 'Ukraine has to want to settle this war.'

Zelensky, who is trying to repair relations with Washington that have hit new lows, said the two sides discussed 'Article 5-like' security guarantees and that he had asked for them to be strong. He also said Ukraine is again receiving US early warnings of Russian missile attacks.

On the ground, Russia's defence ministry said it struck three cargo vessels in the port of Reni and two more bound for Odesa, plus logistics hubs in Volyn and Khmelnytskyi; Ukrainian officials said a separate missile and drone blitz on civilian areas killed at least nine. NATO is deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, drones, radars, explosive ordnance teams and intelligence personnel to the Black Sea after attacks on shipping near Romania and Bulgaria, alliance spokesperson Col Martin O'Donnell said. The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of the military Starshield service Ukraine uses, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the Pentagon 'haven't pulled anything back.'
sections.whyItMatters: The sequencing — Zelensky in Oslo, then Witkoff in Moscow the next day — suggests Washington is assembling a framework and handing it to the Kremlin. Kyiv is being asked to accept guarantees it cannot verify while its battlefield communications are reportedly being throttled.

bottomLine: Three of today's developments share a pattern: air and drone power is doing the work that ground forces cannot. Sudan's army used drones to kill 300-plus people and drew South Sudan into the war; the Houthis used them to bring Britain into Saudi air defence; Iran used mines and drones to hold Hormuz shut at $110 oil. Japan's answer is pre-positioned missiles on Yonaguni. The diplomatic track is alive but narrow — Witkoff meets Putin Wednesday, and Iran says it will not talk until its conditions are met.
